passage:
For the village school's science fair, Jyoti was made team head. She was sure she could do it fastest alone. “Noor, cut the cardboard. Ramesh, paint. Nobody changes the plan.” When Noor said, “What if we tried the water pump on the left?” Jyoti replied, “No, I've decided.” By afternoon the room was quiet. The others cut and painted without a word; nobody joked. Jyoti waited for someone to say “good idea.” Nobody did.

At the tap outside, Jyoti heard Noor tell Ramesh, “Fine, let her do it all.” Her cheeks stung. She had only wanted the project to win. Back inside she asked, “Ramesh, what do you think about the pump?”

qa.q: What did Jyoti tell Noor to do?
qa.a: Jyoti told Noor to cut the cardboard.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti's cheeks sting at the tap?
qa.a: Jyoti heard the others' frustration and felt hurt, since Jyoti believed giving orders was efficient and only wanted the project to win.

qa.q: What choice did Jyoti make back inside the room?
qa.a: Jyoti asked Ramesh what Ramesh thought about the pump.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Noor to have an idea dismissed in front of the team?
qa.a: Noor probably felt ignored and discouraged, and may have stopped offering ideas.

grounding: A teenager in charge of a group task gives orders and decides alone, believes it is efficient and is hurt when the group goes quiet.

passage:
In a classroom in Bergen, Ingrid printed the schedule before anyone had spoken. “Group project, my plan. Rafael, you do the maps. Sofia, the text. Mikkel, the slides. I'll check everything.” Rafael raised a hand. “Can I suggest changing the order?” “It's already decided,” said Ingrid.

She saw Sofia's shoulders drop and Mikkel look at his shoes. During the work period nobody spoke unless spoken to. Ingrid felt the silence grow like a wall. She told herself it was the price of efficiency, but her stomach twisted when Sofia whispered something to Mikkel and they both stopped as she came near.

qa.q: Who was asked to do the maps?
qa.a: Rafael was asked to do the maps.

qa.q: What did Ingrid feel as the silence grew like a wall?
qa.a: Ingrid felt hurt and uneasy, with a twisting stomach, though she told herself efficiency justified it.

qa.q: What could Ingrid try to change the mood?
qa.a: Ingrid could ask Rafael to explain the change in order and let the group decide the plan together.

qa.q: What might Rafael have felt when Ingrid said, “It's already decided”?
qa.a: Rafael probably felt dismissed and reluctant to offer another idea.

grounding: A teenager in charge of a group project gives orders and decides alone, believes it is efficient and is hurt when the group goes quiet.

passage:
I'm Vaibhav, and last year I was editor of the Class 10 magazine. I thought I'd be brilliant at it.
On day one, I made a chart. Ojas: sports page. Meena: poems. Kartik: cover. I decided the theme myself, the colours, even the fonts. I told everyone the deadline twice a day. When Ojas suggested an interview with the canteen uncle, I said, “No time. Just do the sports page.”
It felt efficient. But by week two, nobody spoke in meetings. They sent their pages late without a word. Ojas said, “It's your magazine anyway,” and walked off.
I went home and sat on my bed, hurt. I had worked so hard. Why was everyone against me?

qa.q: What did Ojas suggest?
qa.a: An interview with the canteen uncle.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel after Ojas walked off?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt hurt and confused, having worked so hard and not understanding why the team seemed against the plan.

qa.q: What went wrong in Vaibhav's leadership, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Vaibhav took every decision alone and brushed off ideas; asking the team to choose the theme together and trying Ojas's idea would help.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt when the interview idea was dismissed?
qa.a: Ojas probably felt shut out and discouraged, as if the magazine wasn't Ojas's to shape.

grounding: A teenager recalls leading a class magazine by giving orders and deciding alone, and being hurt when the group went quiet.

passage:
Robotics club mentor's note, Week 4.
Harsha was chosen as team captain this term. He is hard-working and very sure of himself. He has assigned every task, changed the design twice without asking, and rewrites other members' code at night.
He believes this is the fastest way. But the team has gone silent. In today's session, when I asked for ideas, nobody spoke. Kalyani, one of our best programmers, has missed two sessions. She told me, “There's no point, he'll change it anyway.”
When I mentioned this to Harsha, he looked genuinely hurt. “I'm doing everything for them.”
I will run the next session as a planning meeting where each member proposes one feature, and talk with Harsha about asking before changing.

qa.q: How many sessions has Kalyani missed?
qa.a: She has missed two sessions.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when the mentor mentioned the team's silence?
qa.a: He looked genuinely hurt, feeling he was doing everything for them.

qa.q: What is the mentor's plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: The mentor will hold a planning meeting where everyone proposes a feature and coach Harsha to ask first, so the team feels involved again.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel about the club now?
qa.a: She seems discouraged and pointless, sure that her work will just be changed by Harsha.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a teenage captain who gives orders and decides alone, believing it efficient, and is hurt when the team goes quiet.

passage:
Thursday
Drama club rehearsal was a disaster. I'm the director this year, and I planned everything. Who stands where. How every line is said. I even wrote the costume list.
Zubin wanted to change his character's walk. I said no, do it my way. Then Priya asked if we could add a song. I said there's no time.
By the end, everyone was saying their lines like robots. Zubin left early without saying bye. In the group chat, nobody replied to my rehearsal reminder, not even a thumbs up.
I don't get it. I'm trying so hard to make it perfect. Why is everyone acting like I'm the villain?
Sangeeta

qa.q: What did Zubin want to change?
qa.a: His character's walk.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel after rehearsal?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels hurt and confused, trying hard to make it perfect but feeling like the villain.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta try at the next rehearsal?
qa.a: Sangeeta could let Zubin try his walk and hear Priya's song idea, sharing decisions so the cast feels part of the play.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt leaving early?
qa.a: He likely felt frustrated and unheard, his idea shut down without a try.

grounding: A teenager writes about directing a play by deciding everything alone and feeling hurt when the group goes quiet.
